title: The treaty at Hudaybiyyah
hookLine: they come as pilgrims, are turned back, and sign a treaty that looks like a loss

lines: A DREAM OF THE SACRED MOSQUE.
cards: Years after leaving Mecca, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ dreams that he and his companions enter the Sacred Mosque in peace. So he sets out with about fourteen hundred people.

Not as an army: as pilgrims, in the simple cloth of pilgrimage, driving animals to sacrifice, carrying only travelers' swords in their sheaths. They want to do the 'umrah, the lesser pilgrimage, and go home.
But the Meccans block the road. At al-Hudaybiyyah, just outside the sacred boundary, the pilgrims stop. Messengers go back and forth.
In the end there's a treaty, and the companions can hardly bear it.

teach.b: Mecca's negotiator was Suhayl ibn 'Amr, and Sahih al-Bukhari tells how the treaty was written. The Prophet told 'Ali to write: In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate.
Suhayl objected: we don't know this Merciful. Write, in your name, O God, the old way. The Prophet agreed.
Then: this is what Muhammad, the messenger of God, has agreed. Suhayl objected again: if we believed you were God's messenger, we wouldn't be fighting you.

Write Muhammad son of 'Abdullah. 'Ali couldn't bring himself to erase it, so the Prophet asked him to point to the words, and erased them with his own hand. The Muslims go home this year, no pilgrimage.
They can come back next year, for three days. And, the biographers add, ten years of peace.

Anyone from Mecca who runs to the Muslims must be sent back, but not the other way around. Right then Abu Jandal, Suhayl's own son, a young Muslim, stumbled into the camp in chains, begging to be taken in.
He was sent back. The companions were shattered. Umar asked the Prophet: aren't we in the right?
The Prophet said: I am God's messenger, and I won't disobey him. Then he told the people to sacrifice their animals and shave their heads, ending the pilgrimage where they stood, and nobody moved.
He went into the tent of his wife Umm Salamah, hurt. She told him: go out, say nothing to anyone, sacrifice your animal and call for your barber. He did.
Seeing him, they all rose and did the same.

how: Muslims study Hudaybiyyah as a model of patient diplomacy and of accepting hard terms for peace, and the story of Umm Salamah's advice is often told as an example of wise counsel from the Prophet's wives.

o: the well where pilgrims drank on the road to Mecca
the place outside Mecca where a hard peace was signed
the market where caravans traded on the road to Syria

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.
p: go out, say nothing, and shave

s: the Muslims came to Hudaybiyyah as an army
they came as pilgrims, in pilgrim's dress, driving animals to sacrifice.
the Prophet erased the words messenger of God himself
'Ali couldn't, so he asked him to point to them and erased them.
the companions obeyed at once when told to shave
nobody moved, until the Prophet did it himself on Umm Salamah's advice.

games.q: you've told your people to end the pilgrimage and shave their heads. nobody moves. you go into your tent, hurt. what does Umm Salamah advise?
o: go out and give them a speech.
go out, say nothing, sacrifice and shave yourself.
games.why: say nothing, just do it yourself. when they saw him shave, they all rose and did the same.

practice: Think of something you're fighting over, and ask honestly what you'd give up to make peace: not what's right, what's wise, the word you'd erase, the title you'd let go of.
Picture yourself letting it go with your own hand, without a speech. Then look back at this week: Hamzah, the Trench, the necklace, home, children, animals, and now a treaty that hurt.

wordCard.voice: Hudaybiyyah, where the peace was signed outside Mecca: the Muslims gave up the pilgrimage, the title and even a refugee, and it looked like a loss.

orig.note: Arabic: the peace of Hudaybiyyah. sulh, a settlement, a making of peace.

carryVoice: Your line: it looked like losing. Looks aren't the whole story. And that's the week.
